k1p2-14.text: Chapter 1's “model is a mapping” is now a composition of layer mappings

k1p6-37.text: the output is always $-1.5$: not even half of XOR

k1p7-2.text: All linear: any number of layers is one layer

k1p8-11.text: The step works as a nonlinearity, but it is not differentiable at 0 and has zero derivative elsewhere. To learn by gradients, which nonlinearity should we pick?

steps.label: KP05 Stack neurons into layers; nonlinearity gives power
Layers · 1/8
steps.speakerNotes: Connect neurons into layers. The input layer receives the raw data.

steps.label: Layers · 1/8 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: The hidden layer is in the middle and sees neither the answer nor the raw data. Every neuron of one layer connects to every neuron of the next: fully connected.

steps.label: Layers · 1/8 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: The output layer gives the result. Information only moves forward, never back: feedforward.

steps.label: Layers · 1/8 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: o output layer gives the result fully connected, information only forward: a feedforward network

steps.label: Two steps · 2/8
steps.speakerNotes: Each neuron first takes a weighted sum of the previous layer's outputs; this is the linear step.

steps.label: Two steps · 2/8 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: Then it passes through the activation sigma; this is the nonlinear step.

steps.label: Two steps · 2/8 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: A whole layer is written with a matrix: layer k of z equals sigma applied to W transpose times the previous z.

steps.label: Two steps · 2/8 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: the whole layer at once \mathbf{z}^{(k)}=\sigma\!\left(\mathbf{W}_k^{\top}\mathbf{z}^{(k-1)}\right) Chapter 1's “model is a mapping” is now a composition of layer mappings

steps.label: Assembling XOR · 3/8
steps.speakerNotes: A 2-2-1 network: two inputs, two hidden neurons, one output. The weights come from KP01's gates.

steps.label: Assembling XOR · 3/8 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: The first hidden neuron is OR: s1 equals x1 plus x2 minus 1.

steps.label: Assembling XOR · 3/8 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: The second is NAND: s2 equals minus x1 minus x2 plus 1.5.

steps.label: Assembling XOR · 3/8 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: The output layer is AND: it outputs 1 only if both conditions hold. Together that is XOR. The weights are hand-built; making a machine learn them is Chapter 3's job.

steps.label: The table · 4/8
steps.speakerNotes: Compute cell by cell from left to right: s1 and h1, then s2 and h2, finally s3 and the output.

steps.label: The table · 4/8 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: The rows for inputs 0 0 and 0 1. At 0 1 the output is 1.

steps.label: The table · 4/8 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: The rows for 1 0 and 1 1. At 1 0 the output is 1, at 1 1 it is 0.

steps.label: The table · 4/8 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: The outputs 0, 1, 1, 0 are exactly XOR.

steps.label: The table · 4/8 (4)
steps.speakerNotes: outputs 0,1,1,0 are exactly XOR

steps.label: New coordinates · 5/8
steps.speakerNotes: The original four points: the two points of a class lie on a diagonal; no single line cuts them.

steps.label: New coordinates · 5/8 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: The first layer turns each point into new coordinates h1, h2: 0 1 and 1 0 both become 1 1, 0 0 becomes 0 1, and 1 1 becomes 1 0. In the new coordinates a single line separates them.

steps.label: New coordinates · 5/8 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: Only one point has output 1, so one AND in the output layer cuts it off.

steps.label: New coordinates · 5/8 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: (0,1) and (1,0) both become (1,1); only one point has output 1, so one AND cuts it

steps.label: All-linear collapses · 6/8
steps.speakerNotes: Take the same weights but replace the step by the identity activation, which does nothing.

steps.label: All-linear collapses · 6/8 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: Whatever the input, the output is minus 1.5.

steps.label: All-linear collapses · 6/8 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: The reason: the two layers combine into the matrix W2 times W1, which is 0, 0: the whole network is squashed into a constant.

steps.label: All-linear collapses · 6/8 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: \mathbf{W}_2\mathbf{W}_1=(1,1)\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\-1&-1\end{pmatrix}=(0,0) the output is always -1.5: not even half of XOR

steps.label: Why nonlinearity · 7/8
steps.speakerNotes: If every activation is linear, each layer is still a matrix.

steps.label: Why nonlinearity · 7/8 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: Their product is still one matrix, so a three-layer network equals one layer.

steps.label: Why nonlinearity · 7/8 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: A hundred layers are still one linear projection; with biases too, since affine maps compose to an affine map and the boundary stays a straight line.

steps.label: Why nonlinearity · 7/8 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: So the power comes from the nonlinearity between layers.

steps.label: Myths and question · 8/8
steps.speakerNotes: First myth: more layers always means stronger. When all-linear, 100 layers equal one.

steps.label: Myths and question · 8/8 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: Second myth: nonlinearity means it can always be learned. The weights above were hand-built; learning them is Chapter 3.

steps.label: Myths and question · 8/8 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: For the next unit: the step is not differentiable at 0 and has zero derivative elsewhere; to learn by gradients, which nonlinearity?

steps.label: Myths and question · 8/8 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: The step works as a nonlinearity, but it is not differentiable at 0 and has zero derivative elsewhere. To learn by gradients, which nonlinearity should we pick? next unit: activation functions
